outputs.L1:
Lo! ’Tis a gala night  
Within the lonesome latter years!  
An angel throng, bewinged, bedight  
In veils, and drowned in tears,  
Sit in a theatre to see  
A play of hopes and fears,  
While the orchestra breathes fitfully  
The music of the spheres.

Mimes, in the form of God on high,  
Mutter and mumble low,  
And hither and thither fly—  
Mere puppets they, who come and go  
At the bidding of vast, formless things  
That shift the scenery to and fro,  
Flapping from their Condor wings  
Invisible Woe!

That motley drama—oh, be sure  
It shall not be forgot!  
With its Phantom chased forevermore  
By a crowd that seizes it not,  
Through a circle that ever returneth  
To the selfsame spot,  
And much of Madness, and more of Sin,  
And Horror the soul of the plot.

But see, amid the mimic rout,  
A crawling shape intrude!  
A blood-red thing that writhes from out  
The scenic solitude!  
It writhes—it writhes! With mortal pangs,  
The mimes become its food,  
And seraphs sob at vermin fangs  
In human gore imbued.

Out—out are the lights—out all!  
And over each quivering form,  
The curtain, a funeral pall,  
Comes down with the rush of a storm,  
While the angels, all pallid and wan,  
Uprising, unveiling, affirm  
That the play is the tragedy “Man,”  
And its hero, the Conqueror Worm.
outputs.L2:
Behold—a celebration unfolds in the desolate closing years. A host of winged angels, dressed in veils and overcome with sorrow, gathers inside a theater to witness a performance filled with hope and dread. Meanwhile, the orchestra unevenly exhales the harmony of the cosmos.

Actors fashioned in the likeness of the divine whisper incoherently as they dart in every direction. Yet they are only marionettes, entering and departing whenever enormous, shapeless powers command them. These unseen beings rearrange the stage, sending invisible misery outward with the beating of their great condor-like wings.

This strange and colorful spectacle will never be forgotten. Throughout it, a phantom is pursued endlessly by a multitude that can never capture it. The chase follows a circular path that always leads back to the same place. Madness fills much of the performance, sin fills even more, and horror lies at the heart of the story.

Then, among the crowd of performers, something creeping appears. From the emptiness of the stage emerges a twisting creature, crimson with blood. It convulses in deadly agony and devours the actors. The seraphim weep as its verminous teeth become soaked in human blood.

Suddenly, every light is extinguished. Over the trembling bodies, the curtain plunges like a storm, covering them as though it were a burial shroud. Pale and weakened, the angels stand and remove their veils. They proclaim that the tragedy they have witnessed is called **“Man,”** and that its central figure is **the victorious Worm**.
outputs.L3:
In a dark and sorrowful theater, a host of angels gathers to witness a symbolic drama shaped by humanity’s deepest hopes and fears. The curtain rises on performers who appear almost divine, dressed in the likeness of higher beings. Yet their grandeur is an illusion: they are merely puppets, moved helplessly by vast and invisible forces beyond their understanding or control.

The play unfolds as a grim portrait of human existence. Its characters rush endlessly in circles, pursuing desires they can never fulfill and repeating the same patterns of madness, sin, terror, and despair. Their efforts lead nowhere, and every apparent purpose dissolves into confusion. The drama suggests that humanity is trapped within a cycle of suffering, driven by forces it cannot resist and unable to escape its inevitable fate.

At the height of the spectacle, a monstrous, blood-red, wormlike creature crawls onto the stage. It attacks the helpless performers and devours them one by one while the watching angels weep in horror and grief. No rescue comes, and the actors’ struggles prove useless against the invading creature.

The performance ends with the solemn finality of a funeral. The curtain falls, and the meaning of the drama is revealed: humanity itself is the tragedy, and the conquering worm represents death. In the end, death triumphs over every hope, ambition, and illusion, claiming all human life as its inevitable prize.
outputs.L4:
Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Conqueror Worm” presents human life as a dark and grotesque theatrical performance staged before an audience of angels. These celestial spectators watch in sorrow as puppet-like human figures pursue their desires and ambitions, moving helplessly through a drama they cannot fully understand or control. Although the performers appear to chase hope and happiness, their actions are confused and repetitive, suggesting that human beings are governed by forces beyond their power. The stage thus becomes a symbol of the world, while the play represents the troubled and uncertain course of human existence.

Poe fills this symbolic theater with phantoms, madness, horror, and sin. The actors rush through scenes of fear and violence, yet their frantic movements lead nowhere. The imagery creates a sense of chaos in which aspiration is repeatedly defeated by suffering. Even the angels can do nothing to intervene; they can only witness the spectacle and recognize its tragic meaning. Their presence emphasizes humanity’s helplessness, since even beings with a higher perspective are unable to alter the drama’s outcome.

The performance reaches its climax when a monstrous, blood-colored worm enters the stage and devours the actors. This creature represents death, physical corruption, and the inevitable decay of the human body. It does not merely interrupt the play but completes it, revealing that mortality has controlled the drama from the beginning. Once the worm has carried out its destruction, the curtain falls like a funeral cloth, turning the end of the performance into an image of burial.

The final revelation gives the poem its bleakest meaning: the tragedy being performed is called “Man,” while its true hero is the “Conqueror Worm.” Humanity may imagine itself as the central force in its own story, but Poe reverses that expectation. Human hopes, fears, achievements, and sins are ultimately temporary, whereas death alone triumphs. Through its sinister stage imagery and supernatural figures, the poem portrays existence as a doomed spectacle in which decay is not merely the conclusion of life but its inevitable victor.

counterfactuals.output:
## The Conqueror Worm  
*Edgar Allan Poe*

Lo! ’tis a gala night  
Within the lonesome latter years!  
An angel throng, bewinged, bedight  
In veils, and drowned in tears,  
Sit in a theatre, to see  
A play of hopes and fears,  
While the orchestra breathes fitfully  
The music of the spheres.

Mimes, in the form of God on high,  
Mutter and mumble low,  
And hither and thither fly—  
Mere puppets they, who come and go  
At bidding of vast formless things  
That shift the scenery to and fro,  
Flapping from out their Condor wings  
Invisible Wo!

That motley drama—oh, be sure  
It shall not be forgot!  
With its Phantom chased for evermore,  
By a crowd that seize it not,  
Through a circle that ever returneth in  
To the self-same spot,  
And much of Madness, and more of Sin,  
And Horror the soul of the plot.

But see, amid the mimic rout,  
A crawling shape intrude!  
A blood-red thing that writhes from out  
The scenic solitude!  
It writhes!—it writhes!—with mortal pangs  
The mimes become its food,  
And seraphs sob at vermin fangs  
In human gore imbued.

Out—out are the lights—out all!  
And, over each quivering form,  
The curtain, a funeral pall,  
Comes down with the rush of a storm,  
While the angels, all pallid and wan,  
Uprising, unveiling, affirm  
That the play is the tragedy, “Man,”  
And its hero, the Conqueror Worm.
